name: Ornish diet

lead: The Ornish diet is a lacto-ovo vegetarian plan built around fruits, vegetables, legumes and whole grains, with about 10 percent of calories from fat. People use it to lose weight and reduce body fat, which shows in a leaner face and midsection.

It was developed by physician Dean Ornish as part of a heart-disease programme. Studies have found reductions in LDL cholesterol on the diet, and comparative diet reviews discuss it alongside Atkins and Weight Watchers.

paras: Followers eat plant foods with non-fat dairy and egg whites in moderation and avoid meat, fish, poultry, nuts, seeds, avocados and most oils. The full Ornish programme also includes exercise, stress management and group support.

Critics cited on Wikipedia describe it as hard to sustain and note possible deficiencies in zinc, vitamin B12 and vitamin E. Supporters note it is rich in fibre and low in saturated fat. People with medical conditions typically consult a clinician first.

angle.text: People follow it to lose weight; a lower body-fat level makes facial contours and muscle definition more visible. The plan is mainly studied for cardiovascular outcomes.

lead: The Ornish diet is a very-low-fat, lacto-ovo vegetarian eating plan created by physician Dean Ornish, who founded the Preventive Medicine Research Institute and teaches at UCSF.[1] It provides about 10 percent of calories from fat and emphasises fruits, vegetables, legumes and whole grains.[1]

For appearance, the chain is weight and body-fat reduction, which leads to a leaner face, sharper jawline and visible muscle definition for people who also train. Popular-diet reviews include it among plans evaluated for weight loss and maintenance.[2]
A crossover study of Atkins, South Beach and Ornish diets found LDL cholesterol reductions after the Ornish and South Beach phases.[3]

paras: The plan includes non-fat dairy and egg whites in moderation and excludes meat, fish, poultry, full-fat dairy, nuts, seeds, avocados, olives and most oils; fish oil supplements are recommended.[1]

Ornish studied diet and stress in heart disease from the 1980s. His programme combines diet, meditation, exercise and support groups; in 1993 it became the first non-surgical, non-drug heart-disease therapy to qualify for insurance reimbursement, and Medicare began reimbursing an intensive cardiac rehabilitation version in 2010.[1] His books include a 1990 heart disease programme and Eat More, Weigh Less in 1993.[1]

A review on non-drug cholesterol lowering discusses the Ornish diet alongside Mediterranean and AHA diets.[4] A 2020 paper compares the Atkins and Ornish diets and proposes common elements behind their reported benefits.[5] Critics say studies have not been replicated, and the American Heart Association has not recommended it; a Scientific American debate concluded it would probably improve on the typical American diet.[1]

In a randomised, counterbalanced crossover study of 18 adults, 4-week Ornish maintenance phases reduced LDL cholesterol by about 16.6 percent versus baseline.[3] A randomised trial of 174 overweight participants used the Ornish Prevention Diet to test a dietary tracking app, focusing on adherence.[6]

timeline.event: Dean Ornish publishes his heart disease programme book.[1]
Programme qualifies for insurance reimbursement; Eat More, Weigh Less published.[1]
Medicare begins reimbursing an intensive cardiac rehabilitation programme based on his approach.[1]
